overview.text: Pottery is made by shaping clay and hardening it through firing; forms include everyday vessels as well as sculptural and decorative works. Pots may be shaped on a wheel, and artists can decorate them with clay slips or glazes. Firing conditions affect a pot’s appearance and can create different colors and surfaces. The term covers distinct ceramic bodies: earthenware is generally lower-fired and porous, while stoneware is high-fired and can use varied clays. Porcelain is a high-fired white ceramic containing kaolin, prized for its smooth, sometimes translucent surface. Because vessels were made for daily tasks and special occasions, and were often painted with scenes, pottery can also offer clues about past societies and their artistic practices.

key_facts.text: A potter can shape a vessel on a wheel; larger pots may be assembled from separate sections joined with liquid clay slip.
Earthenware is fired at relatively low temperatures and is porous; stoneware is high-fired and can be made from different kinds of clay.
Porcelain is made from a particular clay mixture that includes kaolin; its high-fired body is white and can be semi-translucent.
Glazes and painted decoration can change a pot’s appearance; firing conditions can affect the colors and textures that develop.
Ancient Greek painted pots served practical and ceremonial uses, and their images provide evidence about aspects of Athenian life.
